hints: If water does not cross the cell walls, it must stay inside the living contents - think how the cytoplasm of one plant cell is directly linked to its neighbour through tiny gaps in the walls.
walkthrough:
Picture water staying inside the cells**
Plant cells have walls, membranes and cytoplasm. Water moving in the walls is in the apoplast, but here water is told to move without crossing walls, so it stays in the cytoplasm from cell A straight into cell B.

Name the cytoplasm bridges**
Adjacent plant cells are joined by narrow channels lined with cell surface membrane where cytoplasm is continuous. These are plasmodesmata, too small to see at this magnification.

hints: Water always moves passively from where it is more free to move to where it is less free to move - think which term describes that freeness for water in cells.
walkthrough:
Recall what drives osmosis**
Free water moves by osmosis from higher water potential to lower, more negative, water potential. You can write this as $\Psi$. No energy is needed.

Apply to B to C**
Water leaves cell B and enters cell C, so cell C must have the lower water potential. That difference, the water potential gradient, causes net movement from B to C.
Final answer: down a water potential gradient; cell C has lower / more negative water potential than cell B

hints: Recall the three routes for water in plants - through walls, through vacuoles, and through linked cytoplasm - think which route uses the structures from (a)(i).
walkthrough:
Sort the three pathways**
Apoplast is through cell walls and intercellular spaces. Vacuolar is through vacuoles. Symplast is through cytoplasm linked by plasmodesmata.

Link to A to C**
Because water goes A to B to C without crossing walls, it stays in the connected cytoplasm the whole way. That is the symplastic pathway.

hints: Start at P on the spongy mesophyll cell in Fig. 1.1 - think what physical change must happen to liquid water on the outside of that cell before it can move through air.
Follow the vapour into the large air space and then toward Q - think what process moves a gas through a small pore like the stoma.
Think why the movement is outward only - compare the wetness inside the leaf to the drier air outside at Q.
To get full credit, be precise about location - where exactly at P does the change happen, and what is the state of the water at each stage from P to Q.
walkthrough:
Evaporation at P**
P labels a spongy mesophyll cell bordering the air space. Liquid water in its wall, present as a thin film of moisture, gains heat energy and evaporates to water vapour. This needs the latent heat of vaporisation. The air space is saturated with vapour.

Into the air space**
That water vapour now enters the large substomatal / intercellular air space. This is the start of the transpiration stream leaving the leaf.

Diffusion out through the stoma**
From the air space, water vapour diffuses out through the open stoma / stomatal pore at Q to the external atmosphere. Remember to say diffusion of vapour, not osmosis and not through guard cells.

Why outward - the gradient**
Diffusion happens down a water potential / water vapour pressure gradient, from high water potential inside the leaf to lower water potential in the drier air outside. That maintains continuous loss of water from P to Q.

Final answer: water evaporates from surface / cell wall of spongy mesophyll cell at P to form water vapour; water vapour enters substomatal / intercellular air space; diffuses out through open stoma / stomatal pore to Q; down water potential / vapour pressure gradient to lower water potential in atmosphere

hints: Start with the ruler - measure the length of line X-Y on your printed Fig. 1.1 in mm, then think how to make its units match the actual size given in micrometres.
Recall the governing triangle for magnification - think how image size and actual size are related by division.
Check your conversion carefully - $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ - then divide and leave the answer with no units, just as $\times$.
walkthrough:
Write the formula**
Use $\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image length}}{\text{actual length}}$. Both lengths must be in the same units.

Measure and convert**
Measure X-Y. On most prints it is about $36-39 \text{ mm}$. Convert to micrometres: $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$. So e.g. $37 \text{ mm} = 37000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$. Actual diameter = $25 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$.

Calculate**
Substitute: $\text{magnification} = \frac{37000}{25} = \times 1480$. No units for magnification. If your measured length is slightly different, your answer in the range $\times 1440$ to $\times 1560$ is accepted.
Final answer: magnification = image length / actual length; e.g. image X-Y = 37 mm = 37000 um; $37000 / 25 = \times 1480$ (accept range $\times 1440$ to $\times 1560$ depending on measured length)
